description: Bonjour ! Je suis élève-ingénieure à l'EPT (2e année, aérospatial). J'apporte mes compétences en CAO/modélisation 3D (SolidWorks, AutoCAD), analyse de données, connaissances aérospatiales, bases Python et tout ce qui est pitch. Je cherche : Dev Web, Designer UI/UX et Storyteller
summary:
Beyond the Dust is an interactive web platform that tells the story of NASA’s abandoned space hardware to young learners. Instead of reading about a machine, the child teleports to it: they pick a destination (Moon, Mars or Deep Space) on an interactive solar system map, choose a machine, and land in front of its 3D model.

We integrated seven machines, including the Sojourner, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance rovers, the Apollo Lunar Module and the Pioneer probe. Each one has a story with a beginning, an end and a lesson: Opportunity, for example, was built for 90 days and worked for more than 5,000. Children can explore numbered parts, follow a guided tour told by the machine itself, open an exploded view, take a quiz, and see the machine in their own room with augmented reality. The platform is bilingual (English and French) and offers voice-over, so children who cannot read yet can learn too.

It answers the challenge by turning silent machines into characters, using facts from official NASA mission pages. It matters because it makes space heritage free and accessible to every child, and shows future engineers what past missions can teach them.
details:
What it does. Beyond the Dust turns NASA's archive records about discarded hardware into an explorable story. The visitor picks a destination on a solar-system map, chooses a machine and is teleported in front of it.

How it works.

  • Touchable parts: 83 clickable parts across the seven machines (wheels, batteries, solar panels, robotic arm, rock abrasion tool, RTG nuclear generators, the Pioneer plaque…). Clicking flies the camera to the part, highlights it and opens an explanation with two reading levels (age 8-10 and 11-15), a "why it mattered" link to the science, sourced numbers, and links to the parts it works with. Exploded view, X-ray mode and a narrated guided tour help children understand how the machine is assembled.
  • Storytelling: each machine narrates seven chapters (who I am, why I was sent, how I worked, my hardest moment, what I discovered, my last day, where I am today), plus a timeline, key numbers and its twin (Spirit, Pioneer 11, the Apollo 16/17 rovers).
  • Interactive science: the 2018 planet-wide dust storm, the Purgatory Dune episode, the Pioneer plaque explorer and a light-delay signal simulator (Moon 1.3 s, Mars 3-22 min, Pioneer 10 at last contact 11 h 20 min).
  • Learning loop: a three-question quiz per machine with explanations, an Explorer passport, an offline "Ask me" chat that only answers from validated data, and a printable page for teachers.
  • Accessibility: English and French, narration with synchronised captions (MP3 or browser voice), keyboard navigation, reduced-motion and large-text modes, a 2D story mode when 3D is unavailable, and a light initial download (~160 kB of JavaScript) for slow connections.

Benefits. Children usually hear only about active missions. Beyond the Dust gives a voice to the silent machines and shows how they worked, turning a list of facts into an emotional, memorable story, in a format that runs in any browser, in class or at home, without installing anything.

Goals. Inspire the next generation, especially in French-speaking Africa, by connecting engineering choices (wire-mesh wheels, solar vs. nuclear power, radio antennas) to the discoveries they enabled. The data-driven design makes it easy to add the other artifacts (Surveyor, Viking, InSight, Ingenuity, Dawn, NEAR, Kepler).

Tools. TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js with React Three Fiber and drei (3D), Zustand, Motion, Tailwind CSS, Web Audio API, Web Speech API; Blender/CAD for team models (glTF/.glb with Draco compression); edge-tts (Microsoft neural voices) for voice-over.
